introduces.def: Showing output a line at a time with Console.WriteLine, so you can see what your program did.
A named box that holds a value you can read back and change later.
The kind of a value - int, double, bool, char, string and the like - which sets what you can do with it.
Storing a value in a variable with =, read as "store" rather than "equals".
A special value meaning "nothing here yet" - a type written with a ? is allowed to hold it.
One thing built from a class with new that bundles state (what it knows) with behaviour (what it does).
The blueprint an object is made from - it names the object's data and what it can do.
Computing a new value from existing ones with + - * /.
Joining pieces of text (and numbers turned to text) end to end with +.
Asking a yes/no question with == != > < >= <= and getting back a bool.
Choosing exactly one branch to run by testing conditions, top to bottom.
Combining yes/no answers with && (both), || (either), and ! (flip).
Repeating a block of code - with while, for, or foreach - and steering it with break and continue.
Mapping one value to many cases, each ending in break, with default catching the rest.
A named piece of behaviour you call to get an answer back, so a rule is written once and reused.
A value you hand a method when you call it, so the same method works for different inputs.
One object getting work done by asking another and acting on the answer.
Forwarding a job to a held object instead of doing it yourself.
A method or class doing exactly one thing, so it has a single reason to change.
The special method that runs when an object is created, used to set up its starting state.
Reuse by claiming kinship - a child class is-a kind of its parent and gets the parent's members for free.
Reuse by holding parts - a class has-a smaller object as a field and asks it to do the work.
One call that adapts to the real object behind it, so the same method name gives many behaviours.
Preferring has-a parts over deep inheritance, since inheritance can force a bad fit and multiple parents clash.
Reading a value out of text - int.Parse("3") turns the text into the number 3.
Turning a value into its text form, so a number can be joined into a label or code.
Converting a value to another type with (int) - casting a double to int drops the fraction rather than rounding.
The safe parse: it returns a bool for success and writes the number through an out parameter instead of crashing on bad text.
Dropping values straight into text with $"...", so {name} is replaced by that value.
Reshaping, searching and transforming text - ToUpper, Contains, Replace - each returning new text and leaving the original unchanged.
A fixed-size, ordered row of values you reach by position (counting from 0) and measure with .Length.
Cutting text at a separator into a string array you can measure and walk, like "a,b,c" into three pieces.
Behaviour or data that belongs to the type itself rather than to any one object, so it is shared and needs no instance.
A named value fixed where you write it and never changed, so a bare number gets a clear name.
A field that can be set once - at its declaration or in the constructor - and never reassigned.
A variable that belongs to an object and holds part of its state.
Supplying a fallback for an absent value with ?? (and filling a slot only when empty with ??=).
Reaching through an object that might be missing with ?., which stops at null instead of crashing.
A plain value like int or bool that opts in to being absent by adding ?, like int?, so it is either the value or null.
A type deciding which of its parts the outside can see, marking them public or private.
A controlled way to read and change state through a get and set, instead of exposing a raw field.
A property that works its value out each time it is read, with =>, storing nothing of its own.
A base that describes a shape its subtypes must fill in and cannot itself be created with new.
Replacing a base type's virtual behaviour in a subtype, while code holding the base still calls the real object's version.
Giving two methods the same name but different parameters, so the compiler picks the right one from the arguments.
Overriding ToString so a type decides how it prints, instead of showing its type name.
Implementing IDisposable so a using block runs Dispose at a known point, even if something inside fails.
A row of values that grows and shrinks - add items, index into it, and walk it - unlike a fixed-size array.
A store that maps keys to values, so you look an item up by its key instead of its position.
A type that is one of a fixed set of named options, like a small labelled list of choices.
A small data bundle that is copied whole when you assign or pass it, so two variables never share the same one.
A type meant to hold data, where two of them count as equal when their values match, not just when they are the same object.
A tiny function with no name that you can store in a variable and call later.
A lambda reading the variables around it where it was written - something a plain method cannot do.
Querying a collection without writing a loop, with operators like Where, Any, All, Count and OrderBy.
Turning each item into something else with Select, producing a new sequence of results.
Keeping a program standing when something fails by catching the error instead of letting it stop everything.
A block that always runs after a try, whether it succeeded or failed, to clean up.
Raising your own error to signal that something is wrong and stop the current path.
Writing a type with a placeholder like Box<T> so it works with any kind of value, decided by the caller.
A single method with a type parameter that works on any type it is given.
Grouping related state with the behaviour that uses it and hiding the inside, so callers go through the object.
A rule about an object's state that its own methods keep true, so nothing outside can break it.
A named promise of what methods a type offers, without saying how they work.
Depending on the promise rather than a concrete type, so any type that keeps it can be used.
The real object deciding at run time which version of a method runs, so you add a new type instead of another branch.
C# lets a class inherit from just one parent, so you combine several parts by holding them instead.
Handing a class the collaborators it needs from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of building them itself.
Code that runs your code and checks the result, laid out as arrange, act, assert.
A check that a real result matches what you expected, failing the test when it does not.
Writing a test that passes only when the code throws, to prove it fails on purpose.
A stand-in you control that takes the place of a real dependency in a test, such as a clock or the network.
A test double that returns canned data you decide, so the code under test sees a known answer.
A test double that records how it was called, so you can check the code used it correctly.
Shaping code so it is easy to check - injected dependencies, one job each, and no hidden state.
Code that depends only on its inputs and keeps no hidden state, so the same call always gives the same result.
Changing the shape of working code without changing what it does, in small safe steps.
Code that is open to new behaviour by adding a type, and closed to editing what already works.
A subtype must be usable anywhere its base is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions.
Keeping interfaces small and focused, so a type is not forced to implement methods it does not need.
High-level code depending on an abstraction rather than a concrete detail, so the detail can change freely.
